passages.happening:
The creation week ends here, not at the end of chapter 1. “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array” (verse 1). On the seventh day God finished his work, “so on that day He rested from all His work” (verse 2).

Then God does something new. He blesses a day. He “blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (verse 3). To sanctify means to set apart as holy, as belonging to God in a special way.

Notice what is missing. Each of the first six days ended with ‘there was evening, and there was morning’. The seventh day has no such ending. It is left open.
passages.hearers:
The word for ‘rested’ (Hebrew shavat) means to stop or cease. It does not mean God was tired. God stops because the work is complete and good. The word ‘Sabbath’ comes from the same root.

For the first hearers this was close to home. Israel kept every seventh day as a day of rest, and Genesis shows that the pattern goes back to God himself. In Israel's law the rest was for everyone: sons and daughters, servants, animals, even foreigners (Exodus 20:10). In a world where slaves and the poor worked without a break, a day when no one could be made to work was a gift.

There is also a contrast with Babylon's stories. There the gods rest because they have made humans to do their work for them. Here God rests because his work is finished, and he gives rest to the people he made.
passages.later:
The Ten Commandments ground the Sabbath in this passage: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11). Deuteronomy adds a second reason: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). Rest is a sign of freedom.

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). It is a gift, not a burden.

Hebrews sees in God's open-ended rest a promise still waiting: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His” (Hebrews 4:9-10). Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies today, but all see in it God's gift of rest.
passages.asks: God, who never tires, still stops and blesses a day of rest. Ask whether you rest, or whether you believe everything depends on your never stopping. Rest is a way of trusting that the world is God's to hold, not yours. Ask what it would look like to receive rest as a gift, not something you have to earn.

passages.happening:
Verse 4 begins a new section of Genesis with the words “This is the account of the heavens and the earth”. It tells the creation story again, from close up.

The scene opens on a bare land. No shrub or plant has grown yet, there has been no rain, and “there was no man to cultivate the ground” (verse 5). Water rises from springs (verse 6).

Then: “the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being” (verse 7). God works like a potter, shaping the man from earth. Then he breathes into him, face to face, and the man comes alive.
passages.hearers:
A new name for God appears here: ‘the LORD God’. In chapter 1 he was simply ‘God’ (Hebrew Elohim), the maker of everything. ‘The LORD’, printed in small capitals, stands for his personal name, the name he gave Israel. The creator of the universe is also the God who comes close and is known by name.

The first hearers would catch a play on words. The man is adam; the ground is adamah. He is, so to speak, an ‘earthling’ taken from the earth. The verb ‘formed’ is the word for what a potter does with clay.

Other ancient stories also told of people made from clay. In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, clay is mixed with the blood of a slain god. In Genesis there is no slain god. The man is humble dust, and his life comes as a gift, the breath of God himself.

‘Living being’ is the same phrase used of the animals in chapter 1. The man is a creature, like them. What sets him apart in this verse is that God breathes into him directly.
passages.later:
The Bible keeps both sides of this verse. We are dust: “He is mindful that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14); “all come from dust, and all return to dust” (Ecclesiastes 3:20). And we live by God's breath.

Paul quotes this verse and sets Jesus beside Adam: “The first man Adam became a living being;” the last Adam a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). Adam received life. Christ gives it.

John tells how the risen Jesus met his disciples and “He breathed on them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22). Many readers see a deliberate echo of Genesis 2:7: a new creation beginning.
passages.hard:
Chapters 1 and 2 tell creation differently. In chapter 1, plants come on day three, animals on day six, and man and woman are made together at the end. In chapter 2 the man is formed when no plant has yet grown, then the garden is planted, then the animals are formed and brought to him, and last the woman is made. The name of God and the style change too. Do the two accounts disagree?

Readers answer in more than one way. Many scholars think two older accounts have been placed side by side, each making its own point: the first wide and cosmic, the second close and human. Others think one writer gives first the big picture, then a close-up of the sixth day. On that view, the ‘shrub of the field’ and ‘plant of the field’ in verse 5 may mean wild scrub and farmed crops, which need rain and human work, not all plants; and verse 19 can be read as ‘had formed’, describing animals already made. Readers on every side agree that Genesis, as it stands, sets the two accounts together on purpose, so that each helps the other be heard. These notes do not choose between the views.

A second question arises here: was Adam one historical man, the first of all human beings? Christians answer this differently too, and some regard it as weightier than the question of the days, because of what Paul says about Adam in Romans 5. Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it. The site's Honest Answer on Genesis 1 sets out the main views.
passages.asks: You are dust, and you are alive with God's breath. Ask which of those you forget more easily. Some people need to hear that they are small and frail and do not have to be God. Others need to hear that their life is a gift breathed into them on purpose.

passages.t: A garden, a task, and one command
passages.happening:
God plants a garden “in Eden, in the east” and puts the man there (verse 8). It is full of trees “pleasing to the eye and good for food” (verse 9). In the middle stand two trees: “the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

A river flows out of Eden and divides into four. Two are well known, the Tigris (called Hiddekel here) and the Euphrates. The other two, Pishon and Gihon, cannot be identified with certainty (verses 10-14).

God gives the man a task: “to cultivate and keep” the garden (verse 15). Then he gives him freedom and one limit: “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden, but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
In a dry land, a garden full of trees and running water was a picture of plenty. The name Eden is usually explained as ‘delight’ or as ‘a well-watered place’; scholars weigh both. And it is God's garden. He plants it himself.

Some scholars, Gordon Wenham among them, have argued that Eden is described like a sanctuary, the place where God lives among his people. God ‘walks’ in it (3:8), and the same verb is used for his presence among Israel (Leviticus 26:12). Its entrance faces east, as the tabernacle's did. Cherubim later guard it (3:24), as cherubim were woven into the tabernacle's curtain (Exodus 26:31). And the two verbs of verse 15, ‘work’ and ‘keep’, are the pair used for the Levites' care of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). On this reading the man is a priest as well as a gardener.

The command comes wrapped in generosity. God gives every tree but one, and says ‘freely’. The limit is real, but it is small beside the gift.
passages.later:
Eden echoes through the Bible. The prophet Ezekiel calls it “Eden, the garden of God” (Ezekiel 28:13). Wisdom is called “a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Proverbs 3:18).

The Bible ends where it began, with a river and the tree of life. “On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2). The risen Christ promises: “To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God” (Revelation 2:7).

Work, too, is here before anything goes wrong. It is part of the good creation, not a punishment.
passages.hard:
What is ‘the knowledge of good and evil’? Readers have given several answers. Some think it means deciding for yourself what is good and what is evil, instead of trusting God's word. Some think it means knowing everything, from one end to the other, as ‘good and evil’ can mean ‘all things’. Some think it means a grown-up knowledge that God meant to give in his own time. Many readers combine the first and the last: the wrong was not in knowing, but in grasping at it apart from God.

‘In the day that you eat of it, you will surely die’ raises a question in chapter 3, when the man and woman do not die that day. That question is faced in the notes on Genesis 3.
passages.asks: Work is a gift from God, given before anything went wrong. Ask how you see your own work: as a curse, as an idol, or as tending what God has entrusted to you. And notice that God's one ‘no’ was set inside a huge ‘yes’. Ask whether you see God's commands as a fence around a feast, or as a cage.

passages.happening:
For the first time in the Bible, something is not good. “The LORD God also said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper’” (verse 18).

God brings the animals to the man, and he names them. “But for Adam no suitable helper was found” (verse 20). None of them is like him.

So God puts the man into a deep sleep, takes “one of the man’s ribs”, and builds a woman from it, and brings her to the man (verses 21-22). The man bursts into the Bible's first poem: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken” (verse 23).

Then the narrator speaks to every reader: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (verse 24). And: “the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
‘Helper’ can sound to modern ears like an assistant or a junior. The Hebrew word, ezer, does not mean that. It appears 21 times in the Old Testament, and most of the other times it describes God himself helping his people: “My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:2). It names help that supplies what is lacking. It says nothing about lower rank. The second word, kenegdo, ‘suitable for him’, means ‘corresponding to him’ or ‘facing him’: a true partner, his equal and counterpart.

The word translated ‘rib’ elsewhere usually means a side, such as the side of the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:12). Many readers take it that the woman is made from the man's side: not from his head to rule him, nor from his feet to be ruled, but from his side as his equal. Either way, she shares his very nature.

‘Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh’ is the language of family. Laban says to Jacob, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood” (Genesis 29:14), and the tribes say the same to David (2 Samuel 5:1). In Israel a bride usually left her father's house, so it is striking that verse 24 has the man leave his. The bond of marriage comes before the old family loyalties.
passages.later:
Jesus quotes these verses when he is asked about divorce: “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?” (Matthew 19:4-5). He goes back to God's design ‘from the beginning’.

Paul quotes verse 24 and adds, “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Marriage becomes a picture of Christ's self-giving love for his people.

The same New Testament also honours those who are not married. Jesus speaks of some who stay unmarried “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12), and Paul, who was single, says, “each man has his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7). And Psalm 68:6 says, “God settles the lonely in families”.
passages.hard:
Does this passage make the woman less than the man? Christians who agree that man and woman are equal in worth still read it differently. Some, often called complementarian, hold that the order of creation (the man first, Paul's point in 1 Timothy 2:13) sets a loving headship for husbands in marriage before sin entered. Others, often called egalitarian, hold that nothing here places the woman under the man: ezer is used of God, kenegdo means an equal counterpart, and a husband's rule first appears in 3:16 as a result of sin. Christians differ on roles in marriage and in the church, and these notes do not settle it. What no reading allows is to use this chapter to belittle women. The woman is the man's equal, made of the same stuff, and the story builds to her as its high point.

This passage also speaks of marriage, and it touches many readers in different places. It describes a man and a woman becoming one flesh, the pattern Jesus himself points back to. The church's historic teaching on marriage rests on these verses, and these notes do not deny it. But not every question people bring to this passage can be settled here. If you are single, you are not half a person: Jesus and Paul were single. If you are widowed or divorced, your loss is real, and God has not set you aside. If you are attracted to people of the same sex, you are made in God's image like every other reader, and the church owes you love and a place at the table, never contempt. ‘Not good to be alone’ is God's compassion for every lonely person, and it is the church's calling to be a family for them.
passages.asks: God saw loneliness and called it not good. Ask who around you is alone, and how you might be part of God's answer. If you are married, ask whether you treat your husband or wife as your true equal and partner. And notice the last verse: naked and not ashamed. Ask where shame has come into your life, and remember that it was not there at the start.
